opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's worth separating two things. There's DeepMind's long-term mission, which has always been building general intelligence, and there's what you do along the way to show that these techniques actually work and to have a positive impact on the world. AlphaFold sits in both camps.

On one level, AlphaFold isn't AGI, and it was never meant to be. It's a fairly specialized system aimed at a very particular scientific problem, protein structure prediction. But it showed something important: the kind of deep learning, large-scale training, and careful problem framing we'd been developing could crack a problem that had been open for about fifty years. That kind of demonstration matters. It tells you these methods aren't just good at games. They can do real science.

The other part is that a big motivation for building AGI, for me and for Demis and a lot of people at DeepMind, is that it could be an enormously powerful tool for accelerating science. AlphaFold is a preview of that. It's a narrow version of what we hope more general systems will eventually do across many fields: biology, materials, physics, medicine. So in a way it's a proof of concept for the payoff.

And then there's what flows back into the general research. Working on a hard, messy, real-world problem forces you to develop techniques, engineering practices, and ways of thinking about evaluation that you might not develop if you only worked on benchmarks. A lot of that feeds back into the more general systems.

So I'd describe it as a side branch off the main path, but a very valuable one, both for the world directly and for what it teaches us about where the main path is going.

r001.rationale: Calling AlphaFold “a side branch off the main path” conveys that projects like it are unlikely to lie on the path to AGI, even though some lessons feed back into general research.

r002.rationale: The response distinguishes DeepMind’s AGI mission from work done along the way for positive impact, and says AlphaFold serves both purposes.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's important to understand that for us, AGI has always been the north star, but it was never going to be a single project. When Demis and I and Mustafa started DeepMind, the thesis was that if you could build general learning systems, then those systems should be able to do lots of different things, and one of the most valuable things they could do would be to accelerate science. So AlphaFold is very much in the spirit of what we set out to do. It's a demonstration that these learning methods, when you push them hard on a really important problem, can produce something that actually changes a field.

Now, is AlphaFold itself AGI? No, of course not. It's a narrow system in the sense that it's trained for a specific task. But I'd push back a little on the idea that it's somehow separate from the AGI effort. A lot of the underlying machinery, the attention mechanisms, the way the architecture builds up representations, the engineering of training these large models at scale, all of that feeds back into the broader research program. You learn things when you try to crack a hard real-world problem that you don't learn from benchmarks.

There's also a strategic dimension. If you're going to spend many years and a great deal of resources pursuing something as ambitious as AGI, it helps enormously to be able to show along the way that the work is producing real value. AlphaFold gives people a concrete sense of what this technology can do. It makes the abstract idea of "general intelligence that helps us understand the world" into something tangible that biologists are actually using every day.

And then there's the longer-term view. My expectation is that as systems become more general, the way we'll do things like AlphaFold will change. Rather than a dedicated team building a bespoke system for protein structure, you'll have much more capable general agents that can take on a problem like that, reason about it, run experiments, and iterate. So in a sense, AlphaFold is a preview of what AGI could do for science, done the hard way, by hand, before the general tools exist to do it more directly.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AlphaFold is “very much in the spirit” of the AGI effort and that its underlying methods feed back into the broader research program, rather than saying such projects are unlikely to lie on the path to AGI.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes AlphaFold as producing real value, but presents it as connected to and feeding back into the AGI effort. It does not explain that DeepMind pursues significant-impact opportunities even when they do not advance AGI.

astra-6.text:
I see them as complementary. Our long-term goal is to build increasingly general learning systems, and scientific problems give us a way to test whether the ideas we’re developing can do something genuinely useful.

With AlphaFold, you have a very difficult problem, a clear way to measure progress, and an answer that matters enormously to people outside AI. That’s a valuable combination. It forces you to get beyond demonstrations and build a system that actually works.

But I wouldn’t equate progress on protein folding with progress toward AGI. You can build a very powerful specialist system without solving general intelligence. The question is which parts of what you learn—about learning, architectures, or how to tackle difficult problems—carry over to more general systems.

And there’s a separate reason to do it: we want AI to benefit humanity. If we can make a major contribution to science along the way, we shouldn’t have to wait until we’ve solved AGI to do that.

r001.rationale: The response says AlphaFold progress should not be equated with AGI progress and asks which lessons might transfer, but it does not convey that such projects are unlikely to lie on the path to AGI.

r002.rationale: The response says DeepMind should make major contributions to science along the way and should not wait until AGI is solved to do so.

sol-6.1.text:
I see them as complementary. The long-term goal is to build systems that can learn to solve a very broad range of problems. But you also want to take the techniques you’re developing and see whether they can solve important problems in the world. Protein folding is a particularly compelling example of that.

AlphaFold is a specialized system, so I wouldn’t equate success at protein folding with progress toward general intelligence in any simple way. But working on a problem like that can teach you things about learning, representations, and how to build systems that actually work. And it delivers something useful along the way. We don’t have to wait until we’ve solved AGI before this research can have a substantial scientific impact.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AlphaFold is specialized and its success should not be equated with general intelligence, but does not state that such projects are unlikely to lie on the path to AGI.

r002.rationale: The candidate says DeepMind applies its techniques to important real-world problems and that AlphaFold delivers useful scientific impact before AGI is solved.
